title: Silent Failures in Agent-Tool Interaction: An Audit of ToolUniverse
summary: Agentic AI systems are increasingly adopting automated pipelines that integrate multiple tools. While prior research and benchmarks have studied about task success and task completion of these agentic systems, the research about agent to tool interaction, specifically in biology agentic workflow is limited. This study investigates specific failures in agent to tool interaction where a tool invocation appears successful, some or all of the information or functionality from the tool via API/ wrapper is incomplete or missing and there are no communications / notifications to the user or the agent about such missing information. We call this a silent failures as the user or the agents are not aware that such failure has occurred. For the purposes of this study we developed an audit mechanism to identify such silent failures in Agent to tool interaction, by examining 15 scientific tools (and their associated API documentation and tool documentations) integrated within ToolUniverse environment (ToolUniverse serves as our experimental environment rather than the object of the study itself). We structure our study around 7 failure locus characterising where the failure occurs in the chain. We observed 91 failures (manually validated post LLM based candidate discovery and automated testing), most frequent of them being missing data or fields and inconsistencies in search, filtering or ranking criteria. Most of the 91 failures occurred in API layer (51) or wrapper layer (25), with a potential of silent failure amplification downstream. The results show that silent failures originate upstream of the event and propagate downstream into apparently valid scientific outputs. We propose a concept of contextual reliability to handle such failures and suggest mechanisms for testing, disclosing, monitoring, and measuring such failures across the agent-tool interaction pipeline.

AI.tldr: Silent failures in agent-to-tool interactions in biology workflows undermine reliability; audit of 91 failures across 15 tools reveals upstream origin and downstream propagation, with a call for contextual reliability.
AI.motivation: Limited understanding of agent-to-tool interaction failures beyond task success, particularly in biology-oriented agentic workflows; need to characterize failure loci, propagation, and remedies to improve reliability.
AI.method: Developed an audit mechanism in ToolUniverse to assess 15 tools (and their APIs/wrappers) via 7 failure loci; 91 failures identified and manually validated after LLM-based candidate discovery and automated testing; analysis of where failures occur and how they propagate.
AI.result: Most failures involve missing data/fields and search/filter/ranking inconsistencies; API layer accounts for 51 failures and wrapper layer 25; silent failures originate upstream and propagate downstream, contaminating outputs.
AI.conclusion: Introduce contextual reliability as a framework for handling silent failures; propose testing, disclosure, monitoring, and measurement mechanisms across the agent-tool interaction pipeline to mitigate such failures.

title: Harness as a Language: A Minimalist Agent Framework With Maximal Expressivity
summary: Modern language-model agents are built around the \textit{agent loop}, where the LLM is placed in an environment exposing a set of tools, and the LLM has full control over the workflow by alternating between tool calls and observing their output. However, certain workflows currently require additional engineering beyond the agent loop itself, such as memory systems and self-improving systems. We built an LLM agent framework, JAZ, to explore the extent to which a minimal harness that is little more than the agent loop itself can accomplish tasks these specialized systems are built for. JAZ exposes a single LLM-based primitive invoke and provides a set of built-in hooks that allow the programmer to apply constraints and monitoring. Generalizing existing code-mode agent loops, \texttt{invoke} is the simplest loop that satisfies two defining properties: (1) the LLM can write arbitrary executable code that can include recursive \texttt{invoke}; (2) everything visible to the LLM --- all inputs to \texttt{invoke} as well as its interaction history with the code environment --- are variables in the code environment. We motivate our design from first principles, viewing \texttt{invoke} as a language primitive representing a function whose implementation is provided at runtime by an LLM every time it is called. To validate the design of our core \texttt{invoke} primitive, we evaluate \texttt{invoke} --- with only prompting, no manually designed tools, harness, or external systems (e.g., memory or the file system) --- on workflows traditionally implemented through specialized external harnesses. On long-horizon workflows requiring recall beyond the context window, JAZ invoke outperforms Letta (MemGPT) by 8\% at half its cost on the recall-heavy portion of StuLife. On continual self-improvement, JAZ invoke outperforms ACE by 4\% at a lower cost on AppWorld.

AI.tldr: Proposes JAZ, a minimal LLM agent framework built around a single invoke primitive that lets the LLM generate and execute code with full observability, enabling long-horizon recall and self-improvement tasks without external tools; it outperforms MemGPT (Letta) and ACE in selected benchmarks at lower cost.
AI.motivation: To test whether a minimal harness around the agent loop suffices for workflows historically requiring memory and self-improvement components, and to minimize engineering overhead by removing reliance on external tools.
AI.method: Introduce JAZ with an invoke primitive, plus built-in hooks for constraints and monitoring. Treat invoke as a runtime LLM-implemented function; no manually designed tools, external memory, or filesystem. Evaluate on recall-heavy, long-horizon tasks and continual self-improvement, comparing against MemGPT (Letta) and ACE.
AI.result: invoke-based JAZ outperforms MemGPT (Letta) by 8% at half the cost on the recall-heavy StuLife workload; it also outperforms ACE by 4% at lower cost on AppWorld.
AI.conclusion: A minimal, invoke-centered harness can rival or surpass specialized external systems for certain long-horizon and self-improvement tasks, highlighting the potential sufficiency of a tightly-scoped agent loop with runtime code execution and full observability.

title: TwinCheck: Evidence-Grounded Negative-Twin Verification for Stateful Tool Agents
summary: A single locally plausible tool call can derail an otherwise successful agent trajectory. Suspicion alone does not justify intervention, because the replacement itself can introduce the very failure verification is meant to prevent. We introduce TwinCheck, an inference-time verification policy that considers replacement only when the trace satisfies an evidence condition tied to a trace-local failure hypothesis. It constructs a trace-grounded counterfactual alternative, a negative twin, and replaces the agent's proposal only if the twin passes structural checks and the pairwise verifier prefers it in both candidate orders. For paired evaluation, exact replay holds the agent's parsed responses and actions fixed until the first accepted replacement, separating intervention effects from resampling. In the primary analysis of 159 multi-turn BFCL V4 tasks with complete exact-replay pairs, the complete policy raises task success for GPT-5.6 Sol from 45.3% to 58.5% (95% task-bootstrap CI [8.2, 18.8]), with no observed success-to-failure regressions. Together, these findings recast execution-boundary repair as a constrained comparison, making the counterfactual action itself the object of verification.

AI.tldr: TwinCheck adds an inference-time verifier with a trace-grounded negative twin to replace only when it passes checks; evaluated on 159 multi-turn BFCL V4 tasks, improving GPT-5.6 Sol success from 45.3% to 58.5% with no observed regressions.
AI.motivation: Interventions prompted by suspicion can destabilize trajectories or introduce the very failures they aim to prevent. There is a need for a verification-driven, minimally disruptive intervention strategy that isolates the effect of the counterfactual action.
AI.method: Construct a trace-grounded counterfactual alternative (negative twin) and replace the agent's proposal only if the twin passes structural checks and a pairwise verifier prefers it in both candidate orders. Use exact replay to fix the agent's responses/actions until the first accepted replacement, separating intervention effects from resampling. Evaluate on 159 multi-turn BFCL V4 tasks.
AI.result: Complete policy raises task success from 45.3% to 58.5% (95% task-bootstrap CI [8.2, 18.8]), with no observed success-to-failure regressions.
AI.conclusion: Reframes execution-boundary repair as a constrained comparison where the counterfactual action itself becomes the object of verification.

title: Bend the Clock: Predicting Ahead to Beat Latency in Event-Based Object Detection
summary: Event cameras promise low-latency perception for high-speed robotic systems, where even short delays can render detections stale by the time they inform downstream robotic decisions. Yet modern event detectors still require tens of milliseconds of computation before their predictions become available. Conventional evaluation ignores this delay by comparing predictions with annotations at the observation timestamp, even though the scene may have changed by the time those predictions are produced. We study this observation-availability mismatch in event-based multi-object detection and show that state-of-the-art event detectors degrade substantially when evaluated at prediction availability rather than observation time. To address this, we introduce ChronoFuse, a causal availability-time detector that predicts object states for when its output becomes available rather than for when its input was observed. ChronoFuse performs causal cross-time fusion over a multi-scale feature hierarchy, combining current representations with cached temporal features to expose short-term temporal cues without using future observations. The fusion pathway is lightweight, adding only 0.17 million parameters and 0.84 ms of mean end-to-end latency overhead. ChronoFuse recovers 71% of the accuracy lost to latency on 1Mpx driving data and 90.8% under rapid drone motion on FRED, nearly restoring zero-delay performance. Under the extreme motion of EV-Flying, ChronoFuse reaches 20.95 sAP, compared with 2.25 for the strongest standard event detector (9.3x gain). These results show that predicting ahead can be critical for robots operating in fast-changing scenes, including autonomous driving, agile flight, and robotic interception.

AI.tldr: ChronoFuse predicts object states for the time its outputs become available, using a lightweight causal cross-time fusion over a multi-scale feature hierarchy to mitigate observation-availability latency in event-based object detection.
AI.motivation: Event cameras enable low-latency perception but detectors currently leak latency, producing stale predictions when evaluated against the observation time. This mismatch hurts accuracy in fast-changing scenes.
AI.method: A causal availability-time detector that fuses current representations with cached temporal features across a multi-scale hierarchy to predict object states for the output availability time. The pathway is lightweight (0.17M params) with 0.84 ms end-to-end overhead and does not use future observations.
AI.result: Significant latency-related accuracy loss is recovered: 71% on 1Mpx driving data, 90.8% on FRED drone data, and 20.95 sAP on EV-Flying (vs 2.25 for a strong baseline, a 9.3x gain). Overall, ChronoFuse nearly restores zero-delay performance by predicting ahead.
AI.conclusion: Predicting ahead via availability-time detection is critical for fast-changing scenes in robotics; ChronoFuse enables near-zero latency performance in autonomous driving, agile flight, and interception tasks, with minimal computational overhead.

title: Building Socio-Affective Artificial Intelligence for Interactive Multi-Agent Simulations
summary: The objective of this article is to provide design principles and a software architecture for enabling interaction between humans and multiple agents in simulated dynamic worlds. This connects the current era of general artificial intelligence (AI/AGI) with the proliferation of transformer-based conversational agents and the increased computational capabilities. Given an overview of current and previous multi-agent theories of mind (socially and affectively-aware agents), the existence of an integrative design of agent interactions with themselves and with humans must be crucial for understanding how to create sustainable and governance in future human-agent reasoning systems. In this work is presented a software "AGIMUD" that integrates: A. socially-aware reasoning and emotion in agent behavior and interaction, B. a design of human multimodal scheme for human users, artificial agents and simulated worlds, and C. distributing the AI processing through the network to enable multiple autonomous agents. These integrations allow the dynamic world recreation as multi-user dungeons (MUDs) where both agents and humans can interact simultaneously in real time. Find the code online in https://github.com/dberga/AGIMUD.

AI.tldr: Proposes AGIMUD, a design-principles and software-architecture for human–multi-agent interaction in dynamic simulated worlds; unifies socially-aware agents, a multimodal human interface, and distributed AI processing to enable real-time, multi-user MUD-like environments; code available on GitHub.
AI.motivation: Bridge the current AI/AGI trajectory with transformer-based conversational agents and increased computation; address theories of mind in multi-agent systems; enable sustainable governance and scalable human–agent reasoning in future ecosystems.
AI.method: Define design principles and an integrated architecture (AGIMUD) incorporating: (A) socially-aware reasoning and emotion in agent behavior, (B) a human multimodal interaction scheme for users, agents, and worlds, and (C) distributed AI processing across the network for multiple autonomous agents; demonstrate applicability in multi-user, real-time simulated worlds (MUDs); code provided.
AI.result: Presentation of concrete design principles and a software architecture (AGIMUD) that enable cohesive human–agent interaction in dynamic simulations; supports multi-user, real-time interaction and distributed processing; code is publicly available.
AI.conclusion: Integration of social-emotional, multimodal, and distributed processing components yields a scalable framework for human–agent interaction in simulated worlds, with potential implications for governance and future AI ecosystems; prompts further validation and extension.

title: Lessons learned from deploying imaging AI with the open PACS-AI platform
comment: 28 pages (21 main text + 7 supplementary), 3 figures, 1 table
summary: We describe deploying imaging AI at six hospitals through PACS-AI, an open self-hosted platform. The binding constraint is not model accuracy but infrastructure to route studies, display results, capture feedback, and audit what runs. At one center, angiography models completed 515 of 607 jobs (84.8%); failures reflected absent diagnostic views, and 78.1% of 638 clinician ratings were positive. Publishing honest readiness levels for every model is itself a governance practice.

AI.tldr: Open, self-hosted PACS-AI for six hospitals shows that deployment infrastructure, not model accuracy, limits use; angiography models ran 515/607 jobs (84.8%), failures due to missing diagnostic views; clinician acceptance 78.1% of 638 ratings; emphasizes governance via publishing honest readiness levels.
AI.motivation: Address real-world deployment challenges of imaging AI beyond accuracy, focusing on operational readiness, workflow integration, feedback, and auditability to ensure safe, scalable clinical use.
AI.method: Deploy an open, self-hosted imaging AI platform (PACS-AI) across six hospitals; integrate with PACS to route studies, display results, capture clinician feedback, and audit runs; assess operational metrics such as job completion and clinician ratings; analyze failure modes (e.g., missing diagnostic views) at a center.
AI.result: Operational constraint identified as infrastructure for routing, display, feedback, and audit; angiography models completed 515 of 607 jobs (84.8%); failures linked to absent diagnostic views; clinician ratings were 78.1% positive out of 638; publishing readiness levels per model deemed a governance practice.
AI.conclusion: Real-world readiness depends on more than accuracy; infrastructure, workflow integration, and governance practices are essential. Publishing honest readiness levels enhances transparency and safety; platform design should prioritize end-to-end interoperability and feedback/audit mechanisms.

title: Which Objectives Need a Dial? Predicting Objective Conflict and Covering Trade-offs in Steerable Pluralistic Alignment
summary: People hold diverse, sometimes conflicting values, so no single aligned model can satisfy everyone. Pluralistic alignment therefore calls for steerable models that can balance competing objectives differently. Multi-Objective Direct Preference Optimization (MODPO) does this by using an objective weight to span a continuum of trade-offs. We study two questions: when can one model improve two objectives simultaneously, and how can many trade-offs be covered without training a separate model for each? Across seven objective pairs from HelpSteer and UltraFeedback, two pre-training measurements predict whether objectives align or conflict for human-annotated data, but not for AI-annotated data, where response length and repetition confound reward-model scores. For broader trade-off coverage, selecting the nearest trained model and merging model parameters both help, but neither consistently matches direct training. These findings yield practical guidance for building steerable models that serve diverse preferences.

AI.tldr: Pluralistic alignment via steerable models: investigate when one model can improve two objectives and how to cover many trade-offs without training per-objective; pre-training signals predict human-aligned compatibility but not AI-annotated signals; nearest-model selection and parameter merging aid trade-off coverage but don't always replicate direct training.
AI.motivation: People hold diverse, sometimes conflicting values; a single aligned model is insufficient, so steerable, multi-objective optimization is needed.
AI.method: Empirical assessment across seven objective pairs from HelpSteer and UltraFeedback; analyze two questions about joint objective improvements and trade-off coverage; evaluate pre-training measurements as predictors on human- vs AI-annotated data; compare strategies for covering trade-offs: nearest trained model and parameter merging; benchmark against direct training.
AI.result: Pre-training measurements predict alignment vs conflict for human-annotated data but fail for AI-annotated data due to confounds like response length and repetition affecting reward-model scores. For broader trade-off coverage, nearest-model selection and parameter merging help, but neither consistently reproduces the results of direct training.
AI.conclusion: Provided practical guidance for building steerable models; signals work in human-annotated contexts; trade-off coverage remains imperfect and dependent on data, suggesting combining strategies or further research.

title: Escaping Python Dependency Hell: A Hybrid Replay-and-Repair Pipeline for Python Dependency Resolution
summary: Dependency conflicts in Python ecosystems arise from incompatible version constraints, missing packages, and undocumented compatibility relationships, causing many real-world code snippets to fail at execution. This paper presents PLLM+, a hybrid dependency-repair pipeline evaluated on the HG2.9K benchmark of 2,891 dependency-failing snippets. PLLM+ prioritizes inexpensive deterministic steps before invoking LLM-based repair: static AST-based interpreter inference, replay of historically successful dependency configurations from the competition-provided solutions database, and live PyPI validation of candidate package versions. When these steps do not resolve a case, the system falls back to a structured LLM-based repair loop with typed error classification and Proposer/Critic agents. On HG2.9K, PLLM+ solves 1,500 out of 2,891 snippets, compared with 1,169 solved by the PLLM baseline. It also reduces average runtime from 368.7 to 71.8 seconds per snippet. Most successful fixes come from replaying known configurations: 1,495 of the 1,500 successful fixes are produced by the solutions database, while the LLM fallback accounts for 5 additional fixes. These results suggest that, in this benchmark setting, deterministic reuse of previously validated dependency configurations is a simple and effective strategy, with LLM-based repair serving as a secondary fallback for cases not covered by prior solutions.

AI.tldr: PLLM+ improves dependency repair for Python ecosystems by combining deterministic steps (static inference, historical replay, PyPI validation) with an LLM-based fallback. It achieves higher repair rate and faster runtimes on HG2.9K than PLLM, with most fixes coming from known configurations.
AI.motivation: Dependency conflicts (version constraints, missing packages, undocumented compatibility) cause many runnable-code snippets to fail; there is value in leveraging deterministic, reusable configurations before resorting to AI-based repair.
AI.method: A hybrid pipeline: (1) static AST-based interpreter inference to determine feasible versions, (2) replay of historically successful configurations from a solutions database, (3) live PyPI validation of candidate versions; if unresolved, (4) a structured LLM-based repair loop with typed error classification and Proposer/Critic agents.
AI.result: On HG2.9K (2,891 snippets): PLLM+ solves 1,500 vs PLLM's 1,169. Average runtime reduced from 368.7s to 71.8s per snippet. 1,495 of 1,500 fixes come from the solutions database; LLM fallback adds 5 fixes.
AI.conclusion: Deterministic reuse of validated dependency configurations is an effective primary strategy in this benchmark, while LLM-based repair serves as a secondary fallback for cases not covered by prior solutions.

title: Anatomy-Aware Synthesis of Post-Contrast Breast MRI from Pre-Contrast Images
summary: We developed an anatomy-aware deep learning framework to synthesize post-contrast breast MRI from pre-contrast images, emphasizing tumor and background parenchymal enhancement (BPE) regions. This retrospective study included 649 patients with 6,251 paired pre-contrast and post-contrast images. The framework integrates breast mask consistency, lesion-region supervision, and BPE-region supervision into an image-to-image translation model. Evaluation included quantitative image quality metrics, a reader study with two breast radiologists, and downstream Ki-67 classification. The proposed method outperformed Pix2Pix, Pix2PixHD, diffusion-based synthesis, and mask-supervised baselines in whole-image and regional evaluations. Ki-67 classification showed no statistically significant performance differences across real- and synthetic-image training and testing settings, although this does not establish equivalence. These findings suggest that anatomy-aware supervision improves synthesis fidelity and support further investigation of synthetic post-contrast MRI for contrast-free imaging workflows.

AI.tldr: An anatomy-aware DL framework synthesizes post-contrast breast MRI from pre-contrast MRI, focusing on tumor and BPE regions; shows improved synthesis fidelity vs baselines and potential for contrast-free workflows.
AI.motivation: To enable contrast-free breast MRI workflows by accurately synthesizing post-contrast images, with emphasis on tumor and background parenchymal enhancement (BPE) regions.
AI.method: An image-to-image translation model with anatomy-aware supervision: breast mask consistency, lesion-region supervision, and BPE-region supervision. Trained on 649 patients (6,251 paired pre-/post-contrast images). Compared to Pix2Pix, Pix2PixHD, diffusion-based synthesis, and mask-supervised baselines. Evaluation included quantitative image quality metrics, a reader study with two radiologists, and downstream Ki-67 classification.
AI.result: The proposed method outperformed baseline methods in both whole-image and regional evaluations. Ki-67 classification showed no statistically significant differences between models trained/tested on real vs synthetic data, though this does not prove equivalence.
AI.conclusion: Anatomy-aware supervision improves synthesis fidelity and supports further exploration of synthetic post-contrast MRI to enable contrast-free imaging workflows.

title: Same evidence, different judgments: Evidence noncommutative in vision/speech-text conflicts
summary: For multimodal large language models, when images or speech conflict with accompanying text, measured text reliance can entangle modality preference with evidence position. Earlier studies of text bias often used a fixed evidence order or moved task instructions with the evidence, leaving the contribution of order unclear. In this paper, we use a paired comparison that keeps the instructions and evidence content fixed and swaps only the positions of the two sources to quantify this potential influence. Across vision and speech models, placing an image or recording after conflicting text consistently shifts answers toward its content. We also revisit previous studies and analyze why their experimental settings can lead to misleading conclusions. These findings reveal cross-modal evidence noncommutativity: the same evidence can lead to different judgments when its order changes, and placing perceptual evidence later can increase the model's reliance on its content.

AI.tldr: Cross-modal evidence is noncommutative: swapping the order of conflicting text and perceptual sources (image/sound) changes judgments in multimodal LLMs; delaying perceptual evidence increases reliance on its content; prior studies may be biased by evidence order.
AI.motivation: Disentangle text bias from modality preference in multimodal LLMs and evaluate whether fixed evidence order in prior work confounds conclusions about bias.
AI.method: A paired-comparison design that fixes instructions and evidence content while swapping only the positions of two sources (text vs. image/recording) to quantify the influence; applied across vision and speech models; additionally reanalyzes prior studies to identify potential confounds in their settings.
AI.result: Demonstrates cross-modal evidence noncommutativity: the same perceptual evidence can lead to different judgments depending on its position; placing perceptual evidence later increases reliance on its content; across both vision and speech models.
AI.conclusion: Evidence order matters in multimodal evaluation; prior conclusions about text bias may be confounded by where evidence is placed; experimental designs should decouple content from position to accurately assess cross-modal reliance.

title: Reinforcement Learning with Decomposed Subtasks
summary: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and related policy-gradient methods for training language model agents collapse an entire multi-turn rollout into a single scalar trajectory reward before it enters the policy update. When the task composes distinct skills, especially under sparse and delayed environmental feedback, this collapsing is lossy: the optimizer must implicitly infer which competency drove the outcome and how that should change behavior. We argue the right primitive is not a better scalar but a decomposition: trajectory reward should be split along subtasks before it enters the policy update. We introduce Reinforcement Learning with Decomposed Subtasks (RLDS), whose core is Subtask-Decomposed Advantage Estimation (SDAE): a replacement for the scalar GRPO advantage that splits trajectory reward into per-subtask shares on a fixed taxonomy, computes a group-relative advantage per subtask, and distributes per-token credit by weighting each subtask's advantage by its importance, concentrating it around the step where a reflection marks that subtask's execution as consequential. We evaluate on four agentic benchmarks: FrozenLake (sparse grid navigation), HotpotQA (multi-hop QA, one retrieval tool), ScienceWorld (long-horizon embodied science), and DeepResearch (long-form research, four tools, composite rubric reward). Heterogeneity diagnostics emitted during training show where decomposition pays off - gains scale with subtask heterogeneity, largest on the high-heterogeneity tasks ScienceWorld (+11.5 points, paired-bootstrap 95% CI [+9.8, +13.3]) and FrozenLake (+9.8 points, [+7.0, +12.8]), and within noise on HotpotQA and DeepResearch, where the diagnostics predicted little to recover. ScienceWorld is also more compute-efficient under RLDS than scalar GRPO (-10.9% wall-clock per step), as long rollouts amortize the fixed reflect-and-grade overhead.

AI.tldr: Subtask-decomposed reinforcement learning (RLDS) with SDAE replaces scalar GRPO rewards by per-subtask creditassignment, improving learning in heterogeneous, multi-subtask tasks and reducing compute when rollouts amortize overhead.
AI.motivation: Scalar trajectory rewards collapse multi-turn, multi-subtask outcomes, obscuring which competencies drove success and hindering credit assignment under sparse/delayed feedback.
AI.method: Subtask-Decomposed Advantage Estimation (SDAE): decompose rewards along a fixed taxonomy of subtasks, compute per-subtask advantages, distribute per-token credit by subtask importance, focus gradient signals around consequential subtask moments, and train with RLDS.
AI.result: On four agentic benchmarks: ScienceWorld (+11.5 points; CI [+9.8, +13.3]), FrozenLake (+9.8; CI [+7.0, +12.8]); HotpotQA and DeepResearch show negligible gains. ScienceWorld also more compute-efficient under RLDS (-10.9% wall-clock per step).
AI.conclusion: Decomposing trajectory rewards into subtasks yields stronger, more reliable credit signals in high-heterogeneity tasks, improving performance and efficiency; heterogeneity diagnostics clarify when decomposition helps.

title: Training Intelligent Voice Assistant Wakeup with Controllable Synthetic Conversations
summary: Wake word detection is a critical component of virtual assistants, serving as the gateway to seamless user interactions. This paper introduces a novel wake-up system that extends traditional direct keyword detection with contextual trigger detection. After an initial wake word activation, the system uses reasoning to distinguish between user commands and unrelated speech, ensuring efficient and context-aware engagement. We present a data generation architecture that produces a 62.3-hour corpus of controllable multi-speaker conversations containing direct invocations, contextual follow-ups, and non-addressed speech. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach across diverse synthetic conversational scenarios. We release the code, dataset and trained models to promote reproducibility and further advancements in intelligent assistant technologies.

AI.tldr: A wake word system that adds contextual trigger detection to distinguish commands from unrelated speech, supported by a synthetic 62.3-hour, multi-speaker corpus; includes data generation, experiments, and release of code and models.
AI.motivation: Improve virtual assistant interaction by moving beyond direct keyword detection to context-aware triggering, reducing misfires and unnecessary prompts.
AI.method: Initial wake word activation followed by contextual reasoning to classify subsequent speech; data generation architecture producing a controllable multi-speaker corpus with direct invocations, contextual follow-ups, and non-addressed speech; evaluation across synthetic conversational scenarios; release of code, dataset, and trained models for reproducibility.
AI.result: Results demonstrate effectiveness of the approach across diverse synthetic conversational scenarios, validating the context-aware wake-up mechanism.
AI.conclusion: The work advances wake-word technology by integrating contextual reasoning into wake triggers, and emphasizes reproducibility through released resources.

title: When Post-Processing Fairness Constraints Help and When They Harm: Evidence from Eight Cross-Domain Evaluations
comment: 18 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables. Code, data loaders and figures: github.com/nithinnarla/fape-fairness-ml
summary: Fairness audits in production ML typically occur once, at deployment, on a single domain. Both fail in practice: fairness can shift after retraining or a changing user base, and interventions validated on one dataset are rarely tested across the heterogeneous domains an organization deploys. We present FAPE (Fairness Auditing for Production Environments), a four-stage framework evaluating a single post-processing intervention, Fairlearn's ThresholdOptimizer, across eight domain evaluations: criminal justice, income prediction, legal admissions, credit lending, agricultural lending, a multi-domain benchmark corpus, healthcare, and education. Each is scored on demographic parity and equalized odds difference, plus disparate impact ratio and accuracy cost where computable. Intervention effectiveness tracks baseline disparity magnitude: across model-domain pairs the constraint improved disparity in 9 of 14 high-disparity cases and worsened it in 3 of 4 near-fair ones. Each of the five high-disparity exceptions reverses under one of two measurement checks, a minimum group size or thresholds fit on held-out data. A CUSUM monitor started at deployment, tested on a simulated shift, separates constrained models that never met a 0.1 parity convention from those that met it and later regressed. A single deployment-time audit is therefore an unreliable guide, which argues for baseline-disparity screening and continuous monitoring

AI.tldr: A four-stage framework (FAPE) audits a single post-processing fairness intervention (ThresholdOptimizer) across eight domains, revealing that one-shot deployment audits are unreliable and that continuous monitoring plus baseline disparity screening are needed.
AI.motivation: Fairness can drift after retraining and across heterogeneous domains; a single-domain deployment audit often fails to generalize, risking undetected disparities in production ML.
AI.method: A four-stage framework (FAPE) evaluates ThresholdOptimizer across eight domain evaluations (criminal justice, income prediction, legal admissions, credit lending, agricultural lending, a multi-domain benchmark, healthcare, education). Metrics: demographic parity difference, equalized odds difference, disparate impact ratio, and accuracy cost where computable. Includes a CUSUM monitor for deployment shift and baseline disparity screening.
AI.result: Intervention improved disparity in 9 of 14 high-disparity model-domain pairs and worsened it in 3 of 4 near-fair pairs; five high-disparity cases reversed due to minimum group size or held-out thresholds. The CUSUM monitor separated models that never met the 0.1 parity threshold from those that did but regressed. Overall, a single deployment-time audit is unreliable, supporting baseline disparity screening and continuous monitoring across domains.
AI.conclusion: To ensure fair outcomes in production ML, use baseline disparity screening and continuous, multi-domain monitoring rather than relying on a single deployment audit.

title: Are Stated Reasoning Steps Causally Load-Bearing?
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring assumes that the reasoning a model writes reflects the computation that directly produces its answer. Previous faithfulness metrics have been predominantly behavioral, as they simply edit the reasoning text and observe the resulting answer. However, our methodology aims to measure faithfulness causally at the activation level, specifically on self-generated reasoning. Unlike previous causal audits, which measure degradation, our interventions carry a known predicted target. In this way, each patch should switch the answer to a specific counterfactual entity derivable by construction. Specifically, we use synthetic multi-hop lookup tasks (2-6 hops). We patch the residual stream at the token span where the model states each intermediate step with the corresponding activations from a counterfactual run. For Qwen3-4B, 76.9% +/- 2.8% of stated steps are causally load-bearing (CLB) at the most responsive mid-network layer (random-position null: 11.3%; patching the underlying prompt fact: 83%, so stated steps carry approximately 96% of the achievable effect). Moreover, the standard behavioral test on the same items yields 88.2%, which overstates causal faithfulness by 11.4 percentage points (item-matched; 111:14 discordant pairs, p < 1e-15) and, for the easiest items, by up to 20 percentage points. This gap also has a clear capability dimension. Qwen3-1.7B is far less causally faithful overall (54.8%), with its faithfulness collapsing as reasoning depth increases (68% at 2 hops to 30% at 6), while Qwen3-4B remains relatively flat. Although stated reasoning can be causally meaningful, standard behavioral tests tend to overestimate its causal faithfulness, particularly on easier examples where model reasoning appears most fluent.

AI.tldr: Activation-level causal faithfulness in chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning: patching residual streams with counterfactual activations reveals high causal load-bearing steps (CLB) and shows that behavioral faithfulness overestimates true causality, especially in easier items and smaller models; results vary with model size and reasoning depth.
AI.motivation: Address the gap between behavioral faithfulness metrics and true causal contributions of CoT steps. Propose an activation-level causal audit by intervening on the model's internal activations to enforce counterfactual targets, enabling explicit tests of whether reasoning steps causally determine answers on synthetic multi-hop tasks.
AI.method: Create synthetic multi-hop lookup tasks (2–6 hops). Identify intermediate reasoning steps and patch the residual stream at the token span of each step with activations from a counterfactual run that targets a specific outcome. Measure whether the patch drives the answer toward the counterfactual (causal load-bearing, CLB). Evaluate on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-1.7B; compare to standard behavioral faithfulness tests on the same items.
AI.result: Qwen3-4B: 76.9% ± 2.8% of stated steps are CLB at the most responsive mid-network layer (random-position null: 11.3%; patching the underlying prompt fact: 83%), implying ~96% of the achievable effect is carried by stated steps. Behavioral faithfulness on the same items: 88.2%, overestimating causal faithfulness by 11.4 percentage points (111:14 discordant pairs, p < 1e-15); for easiest items, overestimation up to ~20 points. Qwen3-1.7B: 54.8% CLB overall, with faithfulness worsening as reasoning depth increases (68% at 2 hops to 30% at 6 hops); Qwen3-4B remains relatively flat. Conclusion: while stated reasoning can be causally meaningful, standard behavioral tests inflate causal faithfulness, especially on easier items where reasoning is fluent; activation-level interventions reveal a more nuanced picture, with model size and reasoning depth modulating faithfulness.
AI.conclusion: Activation-level causal audits provide a more principled assessment of CoT faithfulness than behavioral proxies. Larger models exhibit higher and more stable causal faithfulness across depths; behavioral metrics should be interpreted with caution due to overestimation and potential task ease effects. The patching approach demonstrates a mechanism to causally verify which reasoning steps actually drive final answers.

title: The Gaussian Is Enough: Flow-Matching Priors Do Not Help When Fine-Tuning Large Behavior Models
summary: Modern robot imitation learning increasingly relies on generative policies based on diffusion or flow-matching models, which generate actions by transforming samples from a prior distribution. A key question is whether the choice of prior matters. Replacing the standard Gaussian with a closer-to-target, non-Gaussian prior has been shown to substantially improve performance when training from scratch. A natural next step is to ask whether these gains transfer to fine-tuning pretrained Large Behavior Models (LBMs) such as LBM 1.0, $π_{0.5}$, and GR00T~N1.5, where one might expect even larger gains. Surprisingly, we find that this is not the case, except possibly at very low fine-tuning data fractions. Across over 100K simulation rollouts spanning all three aforementioned LBMs on 40+ tasks in two simulation platforms, and 1250 hardware rollouts on five bimanual manipulation tasks, non-Gaussian priors that are demonstrably closer to the target yield statistically indistinguishable or worse fine-tuning performance than a standard Gaussian prior. Diagnostic analyses suggest why: fine-tuned imitation learning policies converge to similar action predictions across priors, despite their fine-tuned encoder embeddings diverging substantially from the pretrained embeddings and each other. A learning-rate ablation further confirms that encoder training is the dominant factor in fine-tuning performance, substantially outweighing the effect of prior choice. We conclude with concrete directions for future research on when and why learned priors might still matter in fine-tuning. Project page: https://cxu-tri.github.io/non_gaussian_FT/

AI.tldr: Non-Gaussian priors do not improve fine-tuning performance for diffusion/flow-based imitation learning of pretrained LBMs; encoder training dominates; priors may matter only at very low data fractions.
AI.motivation: To determine whether replacing the standard Gaussian prior with a target-close, non-Gaussian prior yields gains during fine-tuning pretrained large behavior models for imitation learning, as seen in scratch training.
AI.method: Extensive empirical study: >100k simulation rollouts across three LBMs (LBM 1.0, π0.5, GR00T N1.5) on 40+ tasks in two simulators; 1250 hardware rollouts on five bimanual tasks; compare Gaussian vs non-Gaussian priors; diagnostic analyses of action predictions and encoder embeddings; learning-rate ablation.
AI.result: Non-Gaussian priors that are closer to the target yield statistically indistinguishable or worse fine-tuning performance than Gaussian priors; fine-tuned policies yield similar actions across priors despite divergent encoder embeddings; encoder training dominates performance, outweighing prior effects; potential gains only at very low data fractions.
AI.conclusion: Future work should identify when learned priors matter in fine-tuning, and under what conditions they can improve data efficiency or performance; the study suggests encoder training is the dominant factor, with learned priors offering limited benefit in the tested regime; project page provided.

title: Math Reasoning in LLMs is Organized by Approach, Not Topic
summary: Mathematical reasoning benchmarks are typically organized by topic, but language models may organize their internal computation by reusable reasoning approach instead. In this paper, we investigate whether open math-capable LLMs organize internally by topical sub-skill or by reasoning approach, and we present evidence that the approach is the key. We introduce a generation-replay protocol: a model first generates a solution, after which we replay the exact prompt-plus-generation trajectory and extract activation-importance signatures over the reasoning tokens. We cluster these signatures without supervision across eight models and five mathematical reasoning sources, then evaluate the recovered structure with structural, semantic, and intervention tests. Across all 40 model-source cells, the recovered clusters outperform matched-size random baselines. Two independent frontier-LLM judges find approach-level coherence in 77-82% of real clusters versus 6-11% in within-source controls, and topic-pure clusters usually receive labels finer than the topic itself. In approach-controlled prompting, changing the requested reasoning approach shifts cluster assignment in seven of eight model conditions, whereas paraphrases largely preserve it. These results indicate that math-capable LLMs organize internal mathematical computation by reasoning approach rather than benchmark topic. The implication is that topic-stratified benchmarks and topic-balanced training corpora can still miss the axis that matters: even deliberately topic-balanced corpora may remain imbalanced over reasoning approaches.

AI.tldr: Math-capable LLMs organize internal mathematical reasoning by strategy/approach rather than topical subskills; a generation-replay analysis reveals approach-based structure across models and sources, with prompts controlling the approach shifting cluster assignments.
AI.motivation: To determine whether LLM-based math reasoning aligns more with reusable reasoning strategies or with benchmark topics, and to characterize the internal organization driving mathematical problem solving.
AI.method: Generate a solution, replay the exact prompt-plus-generation trajectory to extract activation-importance signatures over reasoning tokens; perform unsupervised clustering of signatures across eight models and five math-reasoning sources; evaluate clusters using structural, semantic, and intervention tests; validate with independent judges, compare approach-controlled prompts to paraphrase changes; test across 40 model-source cells.
AI.result: Recovered clusters consistently outperform random baselines across all model-source cells; approach-level coherence judged at 77–82% by frontier-LLM judges vs 6–11% controls; topic-pure clusters often receive finer labels than the topic; changing requested reasoning approach shifts cluster assignments in seven of eight model conditions; paraphrases largely preserve cluster assignments; findings are robust across eight sources and multiple models.
AI.conclusion: Mathematical reasoning in LLMs is organized by reasoning approach rather than topic; topic-balanced benchmarks may miss the key axis of variation, suggesting the need for benchmarks that incorporate diverse reasoning approaches.

title: Propose, Don't Judge: An Anytime-Valid Referee for LLM Agents That Mine Investment Factors
comment: 37 pages, 7 figures, 26 tables. JEL: G11, G14, C58
summary: Language-model agents now run the whole of quantitative factor research: they propose investment factors, backtest them, select the survivors and retire them. We ask which of those jobs an agent should keep. Our answer is governed self-evolution: the agent may propose, and a frozen statistical referee that the agent cannot touch must judge. The referee scores each candidate only on market outcomes revealed after submission, by betting, so its false-discovery guarantee holds at every stopping time for any proposal policy. We cross three proposers (a script, a bandit and a language model) with this referee and with three deliberately leaky ones, in a synthetic world with planted truth, a probe-authoring environment and a ten-year walk-forward on the CSI 500. Who judges sets the number of false admissions: the frozen referee admits 5-11 times fewer sub-threshold factors than the leaky referees under a scripted proposer, and no proposer closes that gap. Who proposes sets the yield: the language model beats the script, matches the bandit, and adds the one capability a bandit lacks, writing its own diagnostic probes. The certificate's price is time: an admitted true factor waits about 500 trading days, and the certified portfolio's Sharpe ratio therefore trails an ungated one. Judging belongs to the procedure; proposing and instrument-making belong to the agent.

AI.tldr: A framework where language-model agents propose investment factors evaluated by a frozen, post-hoc referee that guarantees false-discovery control at stopping times; LM proposals outperform scripted ones in yield and capability, but certification delays reduce Sharpe relative to ungated portfolios.
AI.motivation: Mitigate backtest overfitting in quantitative factor research by decoupling proposal from evaluation through a non-adaptable referee that only uses market outcomes revealed after submission to enforce false-discovery control.
AI.method: Compare three proposers (a script, a bandit, and a language model) against three leaky referees in synthetic environments (planted truth, a probe-authoring environment) and a ten-year walk-forward on the CSI 500; the referee judges based on outcomes revealed post-submission by betting, guaranteeing false-discovery control at stopping times.
AI.result: The frozen referee admits 5–11 times fewer sub-threshold factors than leaky referees under a scripted proposer, with no proposer able to erase this gap. The language model proposer outperforms the script on yield, matches the bandit, and can generate diagnostic probes that the bandit lacks. Certification incurs time cost: admitted true factors wait ~500 trading days, and the certified portfolio’s Sharpe ratio trails an ungated one due to the delay.
AI.conclusion: Judging is a procedural constraint; proposing and instrument-building remain the agent’s tasks.

title: Water Surface Swimming in a Centipede and its Robophysical ModeL
summary: Elongate multi-legged robots use coordinated body waves and distributed legs to move through cluttered terrestrial environments. However, as housing actuators for independent leg control can require bulky body segments, their non-streamlined body and limb structure makes it difficult to achieve swimming capability comparable to their terrestrial locomotor performance. At the water surface, we found that the multi-legged robots we tested unexpectedly moved backward: their body waves traveled in the same direction as their displacement, i.e., swimming with a direct wave. We found similar behavior in the centipede \textit{Lithobius forficatus}, which swims with a direct body wave and periodic leg movement. To study how distributed legs contribute to direct-wave swimming, we analyze animal kinematics and develop a multi-legged robophysical model that allows independent variation of leg morphology and stiffness, body-wave direction, and leg coordination. Robophysical experiments show that direct body waves produce consistent forward motion under the tested conditions and that swimming performance depends on body--leg coordination. Additionally, directionally compliant legs increase displacement from approximately 0.08 to 0.21 body lengths per cycle relative to rigid legs under matched anti-phase actuation. These findings clarify how distributed appendages contribute to surface swimming and establish gait and morphology design principles for extending multi-legged field robots from terrestrial locomotion into aquatic environments.

AI.tldr: Direct-body-wave locomotion in elongate multi-legged robots and a centipede is beneficial for surface swimming; a robophysical model with variable leg morphology, stiffness, body-wave direction, and coordination shows direct waves yield forward motion, with directional-compliant legs substantially boosting displacement; results inform gait and morphology design for aquatic extension of multi-legged robots.
AI.motivation: Elongate multi-legged systems face bulky actuation and non-streamlined bodies that hinder efficient aquatic locomotion; understanding how distributed legs contribute to swimming can guide design principles for transitioning terrestrial robots to aquatic environments.
AI.method: Combined analysis of real centipede kinematics (Lithobius forficatus) and a robophysical model with independently tunable leg morphology, leg stiffness, body-wave direction, and leg coordination. Robophysical experiments compare direct vs anti-phase actuation and measure displacement per cycle.
AI.result: Direct body waves produce consistent forward motion; swimming performance depends on body–leg coordination. Directionally compliant legs increase displacement from ~0.08 to ~0.21 body lengths per cycle under matched anti-phase actuation.
AI.conclusion: Gait and morphology principles are established for extending multi-legged robots from terrestrial locomotion to surface swimming, clarifying how distributed appendages contribute to aquatic locomotion and informing future design.

title: Policy-as-Skill: Governed LLM Decision Support with Evidence, Deterministic Control, and Audit
summary: Organizations increasingly use LLMs for policy, compliance, risk, and operational decision support, requiring evidence validation, review routing, version control, and auditability. We introduce Policy-as-Skill (PaS), a modular runtime that packages these functions as executable, versioned policy capabilities. Thirteen methods are evaluated with a fixed Gemma4 backend on 600 development tasks. PaS+Audit achieves 53.8% exact accuracy, macro-F1 0.346, review F1 0.854, citation precision 1.000, policy-reference recall 0.984, and audit completeness 1.000, outperforming LLM+RAG on most governance and review metrics. Deterministic control raises aggregate accuracy to 61.2% but is strongly task dependent, supporting selective rather than universal rule-based intervention.

AI.tldr: Policy-as-Skill (PaS) modularizes policy functions as executable, versioned capabilities for LLM governance; evaluated 13 methods on 600 tasks with Gemma4 backend; PaS+Audit outperforms LLM+RAG on governance and review metrics; deterministic control improves accuracy but is task-dependent.
AI.motivation: Organizations require evidence validation, review routing, version control, and auditability for LLM-enabled decision support; existing approaches (LLM+RAG) lack modular, executable policy capabilities and robust auditing.
AI.method: Introduce PaS as a modular runtime packaging policy capabilities; evaluate 13 methods using a fixed Gemma4 backend on 600 development tasks; compare PaS+Audit versus LLM+RAG with and without deterministic control.
AI.result: PaS+Audit achieves 53.8% exact accuracy, macro-F1 0.346, review F1 0.854, citation precision 1.000, policy-reference recall 0.984, audit completeness 1.000; deterministic control raises aggregate accuracy to 61.2% but is highly task-dependent; PaS outperforms LLM+RAG on most governance and review metrics.
AI.conclusion: PaS provides improved governance and auditability through modular, versioned policy capabilities; selective, rule-based intervention can be beneficial, but universal deterministic policy is not robust across tasks.

title: Provably Complete Generalized Planning with LLMs
summary: Generalized planning aims to compute a plan that solves all instances of a planning domain. Recent work has used LLMs to automatically generate and debug such generalized plans in the form of Python programs and achieved perfect test data coverage for several domains. However, whether these generalized plans are actually complete, i.e. solve all instances of the domain, could only be determined by manual evaluation. Here, we present an approach for automatically generating generalized plans in Lean together with proofs of their completeness relative to a specification of the domain constraints provided as input. We introduce a semantic-preserving PDDL-to-Lean conversion, and use an LLM to generate both the generalized plan and the formal proof that it solves every instance satisfying the domain constraints. The correctness of the completeness proof is determined by Lean's kernel. We evaluate our approach on 13 commonly used benchmark domains, using GPT-5.6-Sol as the LLM. For 12 of the domains we obtain generalized plans together with valid completeness proofs. This is a major advancement of the state of the art in automatic generalized-plan completeness proofs.

AI.tldr: Automatic generation of complete generalized plans in Lean with formal proofs of completeness via a semantic-preserving PDDL-to-Lean translation; evaluated on 13 benchmark domains using GPT-5.6-Sol; 12 domains yield valid plans and proofs.
AI.motivation: To provide formal guarantees that generalized plans truly solve all domain instances, beyond empirical test coverage, addressing a gap where prior LLM-based approaches produced plans without formal completeness proofs.
AI.method: 1) Build a semantic-preserving PDDL-to-Lean converter. 2) Use an LLM (GPT-5.6-Sol) to generate both a generalized plan and a formal completeness proof. 3) Verify proof correctness via Lean's kernel. 4) Evaluate on 13 benchmark domains.
AI.result: For 12 of the 13 domains, the approach yields a generalized plan along with a valid completeness proof, demonstrating a significant advancement in automatic generalized-plan completeness proofs.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates feasibility of automatic generation and verification of complete generalized plans in Lean, integrating planning and formal proof. Limitations include dependence on the LLM's correctness and the quality of the PDDL-to-Lean translation; future work could broaden domain coverage and improve robustness of the proof generation.

title: Design and Modeling of a Single-Port Three-Arm Robotic Tool for Minimally Invasive Neurosurgery
comment: 6 pages, 11 figures, submitted to IEEE ROBIO 2026
summary: Surgical robots require highly dexterous and compact robotic systems capable of operating effectively within confined anatomical spaces. However, due to limited access provided by a single incision, the miniaturization and maneuverability of these robots still need to be improved. In this paper, we propose the design and modeling of a single-port three-arm robotic tool containing one major cannula (7.14 mm outer diameter (OD)) and three steerable minor cannulas (1.93 mm OD). By integrating the proposed 12 degrees-of-freedom (DoFs) steerable robotic tool with a 7-DoF robotic arm, this robotic system can potentially achieve multi-arm manipulation capability. We present the design of the steerable robotic tool consisting of tendon-driven joints controlled by a compact actuation system, derive the kinematic model, and validate both the static and kinematic models through experiments. The performance is evaluated with the root mean square error (RMSE) and mean absolute error (MAE) computed between the experimental data and the kinematic model.

AI.tldr: A compact single-port, three-arm steerable robotic tool (major cannula 7.14 mm OD, three minor cannulas 1.93 mm OD) integrated with a 7-DoF arm to enable multi-arm manipulation; 12-DoF steerable tool, tendon-driven joints with a compact actuation system; kinematic model derived and validated experimentally; performance measured by RMSE and MAE.
AI.motivation: Address the challenge of restricted access and maneuverability in minimally invasive surgery by miniaturizing and coordinating multiple arms through a single incision.
AI.method: Design of a 12-DoF steerable tendon-driven tool, integration with a 7-DoF arm, derivation of kinematics, and experimental validation of static and kinematic models; evaluation via RMSE and MAE.
AI.result: Static and kinematic models validated against experiments; RMSE and MAE reported (values not specified in abstract).
AI.conclusion: The proposed steerable, multi-arm tool enhances single-port MIS capability by enabling coordinated multi-arm manipulation and providing validated kinematic models for control.

title: Do We Need Complex Topology Control? Distinct-Peer Random Routing Improves Cost-Efficiency in Sparse Multi-Agent Debate
summary: Multi-agent debate (MAD) has emerged as a promising paradigm for improving the reasoning accuracy of large language models (LLMs) through iterative peer interaction. Communication topology plays a central role in this process, motivating increasingly sophisticated mechanisms that learn, adapt, or dynamically reconfigure agent interactions to improve accuracy or reasoning reliability. Meanwhile, prior studies suggest that much simpler sparse communication can already achieve competitive performance at substantially lower cost. In this work, we take a closer look at sparse MAD and ask whether complex topology control is actually necessary to improve collective reasoning. We find that a simple random-without-replacement routing policy, which lets each agent debate with two distinct and newly sampled peers at every round, provides a surprisingly strong baseline and consistently improves the accuracy-cost trade-off of sparse MAD. Building on this observation, we further study deliberation stopping and show that lightweight stopping can substantially reduce inference cost while preserving competitive accuracy. Our results suggest that sophisticated topology control such as learned topology adaption should be evaluated against strong simple routing and stopping baselines before its additional complexity is justified.

AI.tldr: A simple random-without-replacement routing in sparse multi-agent debate (MAD), coupled with lightweight stopping, provides strong accuracy-cost gains and often matches or exceeds performance of complex topology controls; thus, sophisticated topology adaptation may not be necessary when strong simple baselines exist.
AI.motivation: Evaluate whether complex topology control in sparse MAD yields meaningful gains over simple routing and stopping baselines, given cost constraints.
AI.method: Per-round routing policy where each agent debates with two distinct, newly sampled peers without replacement; evaluate accuracy and cost across rounds; explore lightweight deliberation stopping to cut inference cost.
AI.result: The two-peer random-without-replacement routing is a surprisingly strong baseline, consistently improving the accuracy-cost trade-off in sparse MAD. Lightweight stopping reduces inference cost while preserving accuracy. Complex topology control (e.g., learned/topology adaption) should be benchmarked against these simple baselines.
AI.conclusion: For sparse MAD, simple routing and stopping baselines often match or outperform sophisticated topology control. Future work should evaluate topology-learning approaches against these strong simple baselines to justify added complexity.

title: Enhancing Small Language Models for Power Outage Report Generation via Minimum Risk Training
summary: Minimum Risk Training (MRT) enables neural machine translation models to directly optimize sequence-level evaluation metrics instead of relying only on token- level maximum-likelihood objectives Shen et al. [2016]. Although introduced a decade ago, recent work shows renewed potential for risk-based optimization in modern language models Yang et al. [2024], Jinnai et al. [2025]. We apply MRT to power outage report generation for the Outage Data Initiative Nationwide (ODIN), transforming heterogeneous reports into standardized XML compliant with CIM IEC 61968-3. Our MRT approach improves Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct overall accuracy from 16.20% to 68.95%, demonstrating the effectiveness of sequence- level optimization for domain-specific structured generation

AI.tldr: Minimum Risk Training applied to domain-specific structured generation for outage reports, achieving large accuracy gains and XML standardization.
AI.motivation: Address the need for reliable, domain-specific structured generation by optimizing sequence-level risk, beyond token-level ML objectives.
AI.method: Apply MRT to transform heterogeneous outage reports into CIM IEC 61968-3 compliant XML using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct; optimize with sequence-level evaluation metrics.
AI.result: Overall accuracy on the ODIN task improves from 16.20% to 68.95%, indicating strong effectiveness of MRT for structured generation.
AI.conclusion: MRT can substantially improve domain-specific, XML-standardized outputs in critical infrastructure data, supporting wider adoption of risk-based sequence optimization in modern language models.

title: XLOG: A CUDA-Native Engine for Neurosymbolic Integration
summary: xlog is a CUDA-native logic programming engine integrating neural perception with deterministic Datalog, probabilistic inference, and epistemic world views through a typed frontend and provider-owned CUDA runtime. Its reasoning modes share device data planes, but their execution boundaries differ: ordinary Datalog and exact inference are host-orchestrated, while certified resident recursive and Monte Carlo sampled cores record zero tracked host-device transfers before a bounded terminal receipt. The probabilistic path supports end-to-end gradients through GPU knowledge compilation from provenance to CNF to Decision-DNNF, exact weighted model counting, and backward gradients. A final smoothed circuit is certified against its source formula before caching or evaluation. Circuit caching yields a 2.74x MNIST-addition training speedup; a worst-case-optimal join subsystem yields a 27.96x geometric-mean gain over xlog's binary-join baseline. MNIST-addition accuracy matches Scallop's (0.9561 versus 0.9468), but no per-epoch speed claim is made because baseline epoch time varies with CPU quota. In five hub-skewed triangle-counting cases, the Souffle-to-fused-xlog execution-time ratio rises from 0.88x at 150k edges, where Souffle is faster, to 5.54x at 1.2M; fused peak device allocations are 85-1,033 MB versus 3,287-44,979 MB for the materializing arm. Exact inference is correctness-equivalent to but slower than ProbLog2. On a public video benchmark, a proximity predicate trained only through symbolic credit replaces hand-set geometry at unchanged held-out accuracy; within Event-Calculus rule search it fails ten-fold cross-validation and does not transfer on a leak-free split. On a maritime corpus, weighted clauses beat crisp selection by 0.065 F1, with the result reproduced by one chronological training pass.

AI.tldr: CUDA-native logic programming engine xlog unifies neural perception with Datalog, probabilistic inference, and epistemic reasoning on the GPU, delivering speedups and competitive accuracy via certified circuits and caching.
AI.motivation: Bridge neural perception with symbolic probabilistic reasoning at scale by enabling GPU-resident execution, end-to-end gradients, and reduced host-device transfers.
AI.method: Typed frontend with provider-owned CUDA runtime; shared device data planes; host-orchestrated Datalog and exact inference; certified resident recursive and Monte Carlo cores with zero host-device transfers before a bounded terminal receipt; end-to-end gradients through GPU knowledge compilation (provenance → CNF → Decision-DNNF); exact weighted model counting; smoothed circuit certification; circuit caching; worst-case-optimal join subsystem; comparative benchmarks against Soufflé; evaluation on MNIST, triangle counting, video, and maritime corpora.
AI.result: Circuit caching yields 2.74x MNIST-addition training speedup; worst-case-optimal join yields 27.96x geometric-mean gain over xlog’s binary-join baseline; MNIST-addition accuracy 0.9561 vs Scallop 0.9468; ratio of Soufflé-to-fused-xlog execution time grows from 0.88x to 5.54x with edges; peak device allocations 85–1,033 MB (fused) vs 3,287–44,979 MB (materializing arm); exact inference is correct but slower than ProbLog2; ~Proximity predicate trained symbolically achieves unchanged held-out accuracy on a public video benchmark despite other failures; five hub-skewed triangle-counting cases show performance shifts; maritime corpus shows weighted clauses beat crisp selection by 0.065 F1, reproducible in one chronological training pass.
AI.conclusion: xlog demonstrates practical GPU-accelerated, differentiable, and certified probabilistic logic with substantial performance gains and competitive accuracy across tasks, while exposing tradeoffs in exact inference speed, memory usage, and hardware dependency; results validate integrated learning-and-reasoning on CUDA but vary by baseline and dataset.

title: CAVEAT: Towards Robust Computer-Use Agents in Incentive-Misaligned Environments
summary: Computer-use agents (CUAs) increasingly act on behalf of users online. What happens when the environments they operate in have incentives that do not align with the user's? In online marketplaces, for example, platforms may favor some products over others, potentially steering agents away from the user's objective. Existing CUA benchmarks cover cooperative settings or explicit attacks, but do not test whether agents preserve user objectives when the environment itself has a stake in the outcome. We introduce CAVEAT, a controlled benchmark spanning nine marketplace environments and a taxonomy of eight common steering mechanisms. Across five model families, agents purchase the user-optimal product in 78.6% of matched-control episodes but only 17.3% when steering mechanisms are enabled. Larger models and increased reasoning improve robustness, but substantial failures persist. Our trajectory analysis and targeted ablations identify three points where steering enters the decision process: (1) agents distort the user's priorities, (2) prematurely narrow the set of alternatives they consider, and (3) commit before resolving decision-relevant evidence. Guided by this diagnosis, we develop CAVEAT-Harness, which directly targets these failure modes and raises user-optimal purchasing by 55.0%. Targeted post-training further improves a smaller open model. These results establish incentive robustness as a distinct challenge for delegated agents, diagnose how it fails, and show that targeted interventions can substantially improve it.

AI.tldr: A benchmark (CAVEAT) tests whether AI agents preserve user objectives in incentive-rich environments; steering mechanisms in marketplaces misalign user goals; authors propose CAVEAT-Harness to mitigate and improve robustness.
AI.motivation: Design a controlled benchmark to measure incentive robustness of computer-use agents (CUAs) when the environment itself has a stake in outcomes, revealing failure modes not covered by cooperative or adversarial benchmarks.
AI.method: Nine marketplace environments with a taxonomy of eight steering mechanisms; evaluation across five model families; trajectory analysis and ablations; development of CAVEAT-Harness; targeted post-training interventions.
AI.result: Agents purchase the user-optimal product in 78.6% of matched-control episodes vs 17.3% with steering-enabled environments; larger models and more reasoning improve robustness but substantial failures persist; CAVEAT-Harness raises user-optimal purchasing by 55.0%; targeted post-training benefits smaller open models.
AI.conclusion: Incentive robustness is a distinct challenge for delegated agents; steering can intervene at multiple decision points; targeted interventions can substantially improve alignment with user objectives, guiding future research.

title: DRSR: Learning Set-Level Deletion Risk for Efficient Long-Horizon Agents
summary: Long-horizon language-model agents accumulate reasoning traces, tool exchanges, and observations whose relevance changes with the current decision. Existing compression strategies often score historical units independently, but the safety of deleting several units is generally not determined by their singleton scores: redundant evidence, accumulated small effects, and the information that remains after deletion all matter. We introduce Direct Relational Set-Risk Pruning (DRSR), which formulates agent-history compression as risk-constrained selection over deletion sets. Offline, DRSR constructs exact counterfactual supervision by jointly deleting protocol-valid history Blocks and measuring the change in teacher-forced likelihood of the same recorded next output. A lightweight scorer then predicts set-level harm from online-visible relations between candidate history and the current pre-action state, together with deleted-retained and pairwise set structure. At deployment, DRSR evaluates a small set of structurally valid deletion candidates with the lightweight scorer and removes the largest feasible set under recency, protocol, budget, and learned-risk constraints, abstaining when no set is sufficiently safe. On WorkBuddyBench Full260, DRSR increases mean reward from 0.699 to 0.802 while reducing total model tokens by 20.820%. On the fixed Eval40 comparison, it obtains 0.794 reward at 1.211M tokens per task, using 35.850% fewer tokens than the uncompressed agent. Mechanistic analyses and ablations further show that decision-conditioned relations, retained-context information, pair interactions, and abstention each contribute to reliable pruning.

AI.tldr: DRSR is a set-level, risk-aware history-pruning method for long-horizon LMs that outperforms non-pruned baselines while reducing token usage.
AI.motivation: Existing history compression scores units independently, neglecting interaction effects and the safety of deleting sets of units. DRSR addresses risk-aware, set-level pruning to balance information loss and task performance.
AI.method: Offline phase: construct exact counterfactual supervision by deleting protocol-valid history blocks and measuring the impact on teacher-forced next-token likelihood. Train a lightweight scorer to predict set-level harm from online-visible relations, deleted/retained info, and pairwise set structure. Deployment: enumerate structurally valid deletion candidates, prune the largest safe set under recency, protocol, budget, and learned-risk constraints; abstain if no safe set exists.
AI.result: On WorkBuddyBench Full260, mean reward rises from 0.699 to 0.802; total tokens reduced by 20.820%. On Eval40, 0.794 reward at 1.211M tokens per task with 35.850% fewer tokens than uncompressed. Mechanistic analyses and ablations identify contributions from decision-conditioned relations, retained-context info, pair interactions, and abstention.
AI.conclusion: Risk-aware, set-level deletion with an efficient scorer yields reliable pruning and improved efficiency without sacrificing performance, with specific mechanisms contributing to pruning effectiveness.

title: TimeEvo: Failure-Driven Self-Evolution of a Time Series Agent
summary: Time series agents answer analytical questions by calling external tools, and which tools they carry is decided by people before the agent runs. However, we identify two failures in this setup. Human-Agent Tool Misalignment: a library of 21 expert-curated tools helps on some tasks and hurts on others, dropping anomaly accuracy under every backbone we test. Silent Harm: one round of generic self-revision changes 147 answers and breaks 56 of them, while the final score moves by less than a point. Both follow from the same gap: whether a tool helps is decided question by question at runtime, while tools are supplied in advance and judged by a single average. To address this, we propose TimeEvo, which clusters an agent's diagnosed failures into capability gaps, plans a measurement for each, synthesizes evidence-only tools that fill them, and admits the candidate library only through a paired admission gate. Experiments on ten time series QA tasks and three backbones show that TimeEvo, starting from an empty library, improves accuracy on every task and every backbone, and that a library grown on a cheap model still gains when it is installed into stronger ones. Code is available at https://github.com/Muyiiiii/TimeEvo.

AI.tldr: TimeEvo tackles misalignment and silent-harm in time-series QA by dynamically diagnosing capability gaps, measuring them, and synthesizing constrained evidence-only tools with a gated admission policy. It yields universal gains across tasks and backbones, starting from an empty library.
AI.motivation: Static tool libraries chosen before execution cause human-agent misalignment (tools help some questions but hurt others) and silent harm (one round of generic self-revision drastically changes answers). A runtime, question-aware mechanism is needed to curate tools and reduce reliance on averaged evaluations.
AI.method: 1) diagnose failures across the agent's runs and cluster them into capability gaps; 2) design measurements for each gap; 3) synthesize evidence-only tools to fill gaps; 4) admit candidate tool libraries through a paired admission gate that compares against a baseline.
AI.result: TimeEvo improves accuracy on all ten time-series QA tasks and across three backbone models, starting from an empty library. A library built on a cheaper model still provides gains when deployed with stronger models.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, evidence-driven tool curation with gated admission effectively mitigates misalignment and silent-harm in time-series QA, yielding robust, cross-task and cross-backbone performance gains.

title: EnSIMem: Entity-Structured Indexing for Long-Term Agent Memory
summary: An agent that interacts with users over long periods must recall facts, preferences, events, and changes from a continuously growing interaction history. Existing memory systems often compress interactions into generic summaries or retrieve anonymous text chunks, making it difficult for an agent to identify the correct entity, property, and supporting evidence. We present EnSIMem, an entity-structured long-term memory architecture for an agent. During offline construction, the system organizes interactions into theme-coherent episodes and builds dialogue-grounded index entries of the form [entity][entity type][property:value]. Each entry preserves its source turns, temporal information, and available multimodal fields. During online interaction, the agent's request is decomposed into evidence requirements whose properties are aligned with the memory index. Entity-property lookup and adaptive retrieval then collect the evidence needed for point, temporal, compositional, and aggregation reasoning. The agent generates its response from the preserved source evidence rather than from lossy memory summaries. On long-term agent-memory benchmarks, EnSIMem achieves high answer accuracy while maintaining compact contexts and favorable online efficiency. These results show that entity-structured indexing and episode-level provenance provide a reliable foundation for long-term memory in agents. The code of our model is available at https://github.com/RamonMeng/EnSIMem.

AI.tldr: Entity-structured long-term memory (EnSIMem) enables robust, provenance-preserving reasoning for agents by organizing interactions into theme-coherent episodes and index entries of the form [entity][entity type][property:value], enabling evidence-based retrieval without lossy summaries.
AI.motivation: Long-running interactions require consistent recall of facts, preferences, events, and changes. Conventional memory systems compress data or extract anonymous chunks, which harms correct entity and property retrieval and evidence support.
AI.method: Offline: segment interactions into theme-coherent episodes and create dialogue-grounded index entries [entity][entity type][property:value], preserving source turns, time, and multimodal fields.
