AI.motivation: Classic visual–inertial filters require parallax and rely on sparse landmarks, while feed-forward depth models provide dense predictions but lack metric scale and gravity information. There is a gap for a system that delivers dense, metric, gravity-aware SLAM with real-time performance and robust startup.
AI.method: Use Depth Anything 3 as a single multi-view depth model for startup and mapping. At startup, form a feature-free linear system from a five-image window and preintegrated IMU, solve it with conditioning checks to bootstrap a VIO filter via buffered replay. During tracking, use the filter’s metric poses to condition the depth model; apply residual scale correction along rays to keep metric baselines; maintain a gravity-preserving submap graph with drift-gated revisits to refine the map.
AI.result: Davio starts earlier than prior methods on EuRoC, reduces localization error, and yields more accurate maps than state-of-the-art feed-forward mappers given the same poses. On building-scale ORI sequences, it matches or surpasses state-of-the-art mappers with the same odometry and shows less degradation when ground-truth poses are replaced by odometry.
AI.conclusion: Davio offers a real-time, dense metric SLAM solution that unifies a single multi-view depth model with a VIO bootstrap and gravity-preserving mapping strategies, achieving robust startup, accurate mapping, and resilience to pose imperfections; code is released.

title: WhatWorkedBench: Benchmarking Experimental Understanding in AI Agents
summary: AI research agents need reliable knowledge of how their experiments change outcomes. We introduce WhatWorkedBench to measure experimental understanding, the accuracy of predictions about component changes after budgeted experimentation. Agents inspect code, select measurements, and submit a response surface, a table predicting scores for every configuration of component settings. Exhaustive CPU execution supplies reference effects for changing each component while holding the others fixed. These effects capture combinations of changes across 36 tasks from 30 data sources and 8 workflow types, with 1248 configuration records. Core evaluation combines 4,206 numerical-control records across all eight families and 108 agent episodes across the original six. At eight new measurements, pair-effect ridge selects an optimum on 15 of 22 sources and limits every effect error to 10% of score range on three. Fitting a Gaussian process (GP) to the same agent observations raises effect recovery, accuracy relative to true effect magnitude, from 0.632 to 0.698 in the original Flash cohort and from 0.621 to 0.720 in an additional cohort. On six completed beat-detection and graph submissions, the same-observation GP raises family-macro recovery from 0.303 to 0.455. On six workflows with six binary options at 20 new measurements, encoding code equivalences, configurations with identical behavior, raises GP recovery from 0.248 to 0.462. WhatWorkedBench supports research on experimental agents, adaptive experimental design, numerical inference, and use of program structure.

AI.tldr: A benchmark-suite for evaluating AI agents' understanding of experimental changes: agents predict score changes across configurations using response surfaces; exhaustive reference effects via CPU, with GP and ridge-based inference improving effect recovery across datasets, cohorts, and tasks.
AI.motivation: Quantify and improve how AI agents anticipate outcomes of budgeted experiments, enabling reliable adaptive experimental design, numerical inference, and leveraging program structure.
AI.method: Collects effects of changing components across 36 tasks from 30 data sources and 8 workflow types (1248 configurations). Exhaustive CPU evaluation yields reference effects; core evaluation pools 4,206 numerical-control records across eight families and 108 agent episodes. 8 new measurements enable pair-effect ridge to select optimum for 15 of 22 sources and bound errors. Gaussian process (GP) models trained on agent observations improve effect recovery. Additional encoding of code equivalences reduces configurations with identical behavior to boost GP performance.
AI.result: Effect-recovery metrics improve: 0.632->0.698 (Flash cohort); 0.621->0.720 (additional cohort). Family-macro recovery rises from 0.303 to 0.455. GP recovery for encoded-equivalences workflows improves from 0.248 to 0.462.
AI.conclusion: WhatWorkedBench provides a framework for evaluating and advancing experimental agents, adaptive experimental design, numerical inference, and program-structure utilization; results show GP-based modeling substantially enhances predictive accuracy of experimental effects across diverse settings.
